claims.claim: chili heat is a chemical illusion: capsaicin triggers pain without real heat
claims.definition: capsaicin, the pungent molecule in chili peppers, activates the same nociceptive pathway that real heat activates, producing burning pain with no thermal energy involved
claims.measured_value: qualitative: pain without heat; no single-number claim
claims.authoritative_source: Caterina et al., 'The capsaicin receptor: a heat-activated ion channel in the pain pathway', Nature 389, 816-824 (1997); Julius, 'TRP channels and pain', Annual Review of Cell and Developmental Biology (2013)
sources: Julius, Annu. Rev. Cell Dev. Biol. 2013
claims.notes: narration stays qualitative; no numeric claims

nuance.note: capsaicin as a TRPV1 agonist producing heat-like pain is well established; the sensory overlap with real heat is textbook

claims.claim: TRPV1 opens above 43 degrees Celsius, and capsaicin opens it without heat
claims.definition: TRPV1 is a heat- and ligand-gated ion channel; its thermal activation threshold is about 43 C, and capsaicin gates the same channel open at normal body temperature
claims.notes: threshold value is the canonical figure from the cloning paper

nuance.note: textbook result; TRPV1 cloning and its 43 C threshold are settled

claims.claim: the burn is a false-alarm signal; capsaicin does not burn tissue at food levels
claims.definition: at dietary doses capsaicin activates pain neurons without causing thermal injury; the sensation of burning occurs without tissue damage, though very high concentrations can irritate or desensitize
claims.measured_value: qualitative: no thermal injury at food doses
claims.authoritative_source: Julius, 'TRP channels and pain', Annu Rev Cell Dev Biol 29, 355-384 (2013); Szallasi & Blumberg, 'vanilloid (capsaicin) receptors and mechanisms', Pharmacological Reviews (1999)
claims.notes: narration hedges with 'at the levels we eat'; concentrated extracts are excluded

nuance.note: pain-without-damage at dietary levels is standard; scope limited to food doses by narration

claims.claim: capsaicin is fat-soluble, so water spreads it rather than washing it away
claims.definition: capsaicin is a hydrophobic vanilloid lipid; it partitions into oils and fats and is poorly soluble in water, so water rinsing redistributes it on mucosal surfaces
claims.authoritative_source: Szallasi & Blumberg, Pharmacological Reviews 51(2), 159-212 (1999); material safety and solubility data for capsaicin (practically insoluble in water, freely soluble in ethanol/fat)
claims.notes: hydrophobicity of the molecule is a settled chemical property

claims.claim: milk casein binds capsaicin and tends to wash it away better than water
claims.definition: casein micelles in milk can bind lipophilic capsaicin; sensory studies found milk reduces oral burn more effectively than water, though effect sizes are modest and partly studied in small panels
claims.measured_value: qualitative: milk outperforms water in rinse trials
claims.authoritative_source: Nasrawi & Pangborn, 'Temporal effectiveness of mouth-rinsing on capsaicin mouth-burn', Physiology & Behavior 47(3), 617-621 (1990); later sensory-comparison work (e.g., Beer vs dairy trials)
claims.notes: narration hedges with 'tends to work better'

nuance.note: direction of effect is consistent across trials; casein-binding mechanism is broadly accepted but partly inferred from hydrophobicity

claims.claim: bird TRPV1 is insensitive to capsaicin
claims.definition: avian TRPV1 differs from mammalian TRPV1 at a few key residues; the avian receptor responds to heat but is not gated by capsaicin, so birds do not perceive chili burn
claims.measured_value: qualitative: capsaicin insensitivity of avian TRPV1
claims.authoritative_source: Jordt & Julius, 'Molecular basis for species-specific sensitivity to hot chili peppers', Cell 108, 421-430 (2002)

nuance.note: species-specific capsaicin resistance of bird TRPV1 is well established

claims.claim: the burn is thought to filter seed dispersers: deter mammals, keep birds
claims.definition: capsaicin is proposed to be an anti-mammalian defense: mammals crush seeds with molars while birds swallow them intact and disperse them; direct field evidence exists for fungal defense and mammal deterrence, with the disperser-filter picture supported but multi-causal
claims.measured_value: qualitative evolutionary explanation; no single-number claim
claims.authoritative_source: Jordt & Julius, Cell (2002) (species-specific sensitivity); Tewksbury & Nabhan, 'Seed dispersal: directed deterrence by capsaicin in chillies', Nature 412, 403-404 (2001); Levey et al., 'A field test of the directed deterrence hypothesis in a wild pepper', PNAS (2006)
claims.notes: narration hedges with 'one leading explanation says'; directed deterrence has field support but is not the only proposed driver (fungi, pathogens)

nuance.note: directed deterrence is evidence-backed (Nature 2001, PNAS 2006) but multi-causal: fungal defense also implicated; narration keeps 'one leading explanation'
